rationale: I'm replacing the 5 broad bands with log relative power in 2-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz. The broad bands blur known schizophrenia changes such as slowing of the alpha peak, the alpha/theta boundary and the theta/beta subbands, while finer bins keep them. Because this makes far more features, the logistic regularization strength C is chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few eye-movement, muscle or electrode-pop segments can dominate the mean Welch spectrum (especially delta and gamma, which are where schizophrenia effects are also expected). I'm switching to median averaging across Welch segments. This is a robust, per-epoch way of handling artifacts that keeps the background spectrum and should also carry over better to the shorter, noisier external recordings.

I'm adding Riemannian tangent-space features of the spatial covariance matrix to the existing log relative band power. The covariance is computed after average re-referencing, a 1-45 Hz band-pass and OAS shrinkage, and each matrix is divided by its trace so that only the spatial structure is kept. Schizophrenia is linked to changed large-scale functional connectivity, which band power alone does not capture. Dividing by the trace and re-referencing should make these features hold up across amplifier scales and original references on the external sets.

I'm replacing the single broadband covariance with a filter bank: tangent-space covariances for 1–45 Hz plus delta, theta, alpha and beta separately. Connectivity changes in schizophrenia are band-specific (more slow-wave coupling, less alpha coupling), and a broadband covariance mostly reflects alpha, so it blurs them. The new band blocks are down-weighted by 1/sqrt(4) after standardization. Together they then carry about as much prior weight as one block, which keeps the logistic model from being swamped by the extra features.

I'm adding a small spectral-shape block per channel and condition: the aperiodic 1/f exponent and the individual alpha peak frequency. The exponent is a log-log linear fit over 2–40 Hz that leaves out 7–14 Hz. The peak frequency is the centre of gravity of the periodic residual between 7 and 13 Hz. Both are reported to change in schizophrenia (a different E/I-balance slope and a slower alpha peak), the current band and covariance features don't measure either one directly, and both stay the same when amplitude scale changes. The new block is standardized and given the weight of one block.

I'm adding a block of signal-complexity features: per-channel Higuchi and Katz fractal dimension of the 1–45 Hz average-referenced EEG, computed in 4-s epochs and summarized by the median across epochs. Altered EEG complexity is one of the most consistently reported resting-state markers of schizophrenia, including on RepOD, and none of the current spectral or covariance features measure it. Both measures stay the same when amplitude scale changes, and taking the median over epochs makes them robust to artifacts and to the shorter external recordings; the block is standardized and given the weight of one block.

I'm adding phase-synchrony features. For each channel pair (120 pairs), I compute the weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) from the Hilbert analytic signal of the average-referenced EEG, in four bands: delta, theta, alpha and beta. Each band block is standardized and down-weighted by 1/sqrt(4), so the four blocks together carry about one block's weight. The current covariance features are dominated by zero-lag coupling, which mostly reflects volume conduction. wPLI uses only non-zero-lag phase coupling, which is the kind of connectivity reported to be disrupted in schizophrenia. Volume conduction and the recording reference affect it much less, and amplitude scale not at all, so it should transfer better to the external amplifiers.

I'm adding an EEG microstate block. Four polarity-invariant templates are fitted label-free with modified k-means on GFP peaks pooled across all subjects (2–20 Hz, average reference). Each subject is then backfitted to these templates to get, per class, coverage, mean duration and occurrence rate, plus transition probabilities and GEV. Altered microstate dynamics, especially more class C and less class D, are among the most replicated resting-state findings in schizophrenia. The current spectral, covariance and wPLI features don't measure these sub-second spatial dynamics. The new block does not depend on amplitude scale or recording length.

I'm adding a block of orthogonalized amplitude-envelope correlations (AEC-c, Hipp et al. 2012) for all 120 channel pairs in delta, theta, alpha and beta. The signals are average-referenced and the correlations Fisher-z transformed. Each band block is down-weighted by 1/sqrt(4), so the four together carry about one block's weight. The current features capture zero-lag covariance and non-zero-lag phase coupling (wPLI), but not slow co-fluctuation of band-limited power between regions. That is a separate kind of coupling, reported to be disrupted in schizophrenia. Orthogonalizing removes zero-lag leakage from volume conduction and the reference, and correlation does not depend on amplitude scale, so the block should hold up on the external sets.

The relative band power and spectral-shape blocks (1/f exponent, alpha peak frequency) are the only features still computed on each recording's original reference. All the covariance, wPLI and microstate features already use the average reference. I'm switching these two blocks to the average reference as well. Reference-dependent spectra pick up power from the reference electrode, which differs between clinics, so this should reduce site-specific bias and transfer better to MSU and RepOD.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few high-amplitude segments (eye movements, muscle bursts, electrode pops) can dominate the second-order covariance statistics behind the filter-bank tangent-space blocks, which are the strongest feature family. I'm adding robust epoch rejection to the covariance features only. Each recording is split into 2-s epochs. Each epoch's broadband (1–45 Hz) log-variance per channel is z-scored against that channel's median and MAD across epochs. Epochs where any channel's z-score is above 3 are dropped, and the remaining clean samples are used for every band's OAS covariance. This should sharpen the connectivity signal and make it more robust on the shorter, noisier external recordings.

Rejecting artifact epochs helped the covariance blocks in round 11. This change reuses that same clean-epoch mask for the wPLI phase-lag features and the microstate features (GFP-peak template fitting and per-subject backfitting). High-amplitude eye, muscle and electrode-pop bursts otherwise dominate the imaginary cross-spectrum sums and the GFP peaks, which biases connectivity and microstate statistics. Excluding them should sharpen these blocks and make them hold up better on the shorter, noisier external recordings.

I'm adding a fifth sub-band, low gamma (30–45 Hz), to the Riemannian covariance filter bank. Resting-state gamma abnormalities are one of the more consistent electrophysiological signs of NMDA/PV-interneuron dysfunction in schizophrenia. Right now gamma enters only as per-channel relative power, so its spatial coupling structure is never seen. The new block reuses the artifact-free epoch mask and trace normalization, and the sub-band weight changes from 1/sqrt(4) to 1/sqrt(5) so the sub-band blocks together still carry about one block's prior weight.

I'm adding low gamma (30–45 Hz) as a fifth wPLI phase-lag band, so the wPLI blocks match the covariance filter bank that gained from gamma in round 13. Disrupted gamma-band phase synchronization is a core NMDA/PV-interneuron finding in schizophrenia, and so far gamma enters only as zero-lag covariance and relative power. The wPLI down-weight updates automatically to 1/sqrt(5), so the five band blocks together still carry about one block's prior weight.

I'm adding long-range temporal correlations: a per-channel detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) exponent of the alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) amplitude envelopes, computed on average-referenced EEG over 1–10 s windows. Nikulin et al. (2012) reported weaker scale-free alpha/beta amplitude dynamics in schizophrenia, and none of the current spectral, covariance, wPLI or microstate features measure these slow amplitude fluctuations. The exponent does not depend on amplitude scale, and the fixed 1–10 s window range still works on the 1-min external recordings.

In the Riemannian covariance filter bank, I'm replacing the single alpha band (8–13 Hz) with lower alpha (8–10 Hz) and upper alpha (10–13 Hz). The alpha peak is slower in schizophrenia, and the two halves have different generators and topographies (low alpha is widespread, upper alpha is posterior and task-related). One trace-normalized 8–13 Hz covariance mixes these and hides the shift in spatial coupling. The sub-band down-weight updates automatically to 1/sqrt(6), so all sub-band blocks together still carry about one block's prior weight.

I'm adding a per-channel cross-frequency phase–amplitude coupling (PAC) block, a feature type none of the earlier rounds tried. For each channel I compute the amplitude-normalized mean-vector length between a slow phase and a faster amplitude: delta, theta and alpha phase coupled to low-gamma (30–45 Hz) amplitude, and theta phase coupled to beta amplitude, on average-referenced EEG. The hypothesis is that NMDA/PV-interneuron dysfunction in schizophrenia disrupts how slow rhythms nest faster ones. None of the current features measure that, because power, covariance, wPLI and microstates each look within one band. Dividing by mean amplitude makes the measure independent of amplitude scale, and it works on 1-min recordings. The block is standardized and given the weight of one block.

Split the beta covariance sub-band (13–30 Hz) into low beta (13–20 Hz) and high beta (20–30 Hz). Splitting alpha the same way helped in round 16, and schizophrenia studies report changes in beta-2 power and coupling (thought to reflect cortical hyperarousal and medication effects) that differ in topography from the more widespread beta-1 rhythm. A single trace-normalized 13–30 Hz covariance mixes the two. The sub-band down-weight updates automatically to 1/sqrt(7), so all sub-band blocks together still carry about one block's prior weight.

`C=0.1` was set when the model had about 100 features. It now has about 1,500, with the covariance filter bank, wPLI and microstate blocks, so the right amount of shrinkage has probably moved. This change picks `C` from a small grid (0.02–0.5) by inner 5-fold CV grouped by `groups_train` on each training fold, using the AUROC of the pooled inner out-of-fold predictions. Ties go to the smaller `C`, i.e. stronger regularization. The scalers and tangent-space reference are still fitted once on the outer training fold, without labels. In round 1, inner-CV tuning of `C` was tried together with 2-Hz bins and the round was discarded, so tuning `C` on its own is still untested. That result is a mild warning that this could lower the score.
